items.title: Sub-Part 18: Four Yokes That Only a Non-Returner Can Truly Cast Off

items.zh: 若有熏除諸尋思，於內無餘離分別；超過礙著、諸色想；四軛蠲除、不往生。
items.en: If one purges every rumination, becomes, within, entirely free of discursive thought, and passes beyond what obstructs and binds and beyond all perceptions of form — the four yokes cast off, one is reborn [in the lower realms] no more.

items.zh: 此頌所明，謂如有一，已入有學位，未離欲界欲。依初靜慮，熏除欲界諸惡尋思。依第二靜慮，內等清淨心一趣性，初靜慮地所有分別無餘永離，無復分別。依第三靜慮，超過第二靜慮地諸喜礙著；依第四靜慮，超過第三靜慮地諸樂礙著。依無色定，超過一切所有色想。如是漸次，因依諸定，乃至有頂若定、若生，蠲除四軛。何等為四？一、蠲除染污尋思軛，二、蠲除不染污尋思軛，三、蠲除喜樂繫縛軛，四、蠲除一切色想軛。由此因緣，於諸下地不復往生。當知異生雖到有頂若定、若生，猶為四軛所繫縛故，於諸下地還復往生。復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂薄伽梵此中略示，到有邊際有學、異生二種差別。當知是名此中略義。

items.title: Sub-Part 19: Four Practices That Ripen Pure Faith Into Nirvāṇa

items.zh: 惠施令福增，防非滅怨害，修善捨諸惡，惑盡得涅槃。
items.en: Generosity increases merit; guarding against wrongdoing dissolves enmity and harm; cultivating what is wholesome relinquishes every evil; and the exhaustion of affliction attains nirvāṇa.

items.zh: 此頌所明，謂如有一，於佛所證法毘奈耶獲得正信，雖處居家，而心遠離慳垢纏縛，受持七種依福業事。由此因緣，若行、若住，廣說如經，乃至生長如是福德。若有復能於善說法毘奈耶中清淨出家。既出家已，具足忍力，為護尸羅，雖遭他罵、侵惱、訶責，或以身手、瓦礫、刀杖歐擊傷害；恐壞尸羅，當為障礙，心無惡念，不出惡言，唯緣彼境與慈俱心，於一切方遍滿而住。由此因緣，於現法中自他相續所有怨害，並皆止息；當生無惱樂世界中，無多怨敵，為世欣仰，眾所樂見。如是善修正方便已，依增上戒起增上心，依增上心發增上慧。當於聖諦入現觀時，則能永捨趣惡趣業及諸惡趣。又修如先所得道故，漸次永除所有諸結，於有餘依涅槃界中而般涅槃。如是後時，於無餘依涅槃界中，復般涅槃。復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂薄伽梵此中略示，得淨信者四種正行。一、感財富行；二、感善趣行，三、離惡趣苦，清淨修行；四、離一切苦，清淨修行。當知是名此中略義。

items.title: Sub-Part 20: The Teaching Shared by No Other Tradition

items.zh: 諸惡者莫作，諸善者奉行，自調伏其心，是諸佛聖教。
items.en: Do not commit any evil; uphold and practice every good; tame your own mind completely — this is the teaching of all buddhas.

items.zh: 此頌所明，謂如有一，於佛所證法毘奈耶獲得正信，於一切種、一切因緣、一切處所所有惡行，皆能斷滅；於善說法毘奈耶中，能善受學尸羅律儀。彼由三相奉行諸善。謂善住尸羅，守別解脫清淨律儀，乃至受學所有學處。依增上戒學發增上心學，依增上心學發增上慧學；彼由此故，於所知境如實知見。如是具足諸善法已，復由三相調伏自心。謂如實知故，能起厭患；由厭患故，能得離染；由離染故，能得解脫。復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂薄伽梵此中略示，三學學果、顯自聖教不與他共。當知是名此中略義。

blocks.text: Three verses, the last one perhaps the best known in all Buddhism. The explanations are **untranslated**.
"Purging every rumination, free within of discursive thought, passing beyond every obstruction and all perceptions of form: the four yokes cast off, one never returns to birth."

The prose: a trainee not yet free of sense desire uses the first dhyāna to purge unwholesome thoughts; the second, to go beyond all discursive thought; the third and fourth, to pass beyond the attachments of joy and of pleasure; the formless attainments, to pass beyond all perceptions of form. Four yokes are cast off: defiled thought, undefiled thought, bondage to joy and pleasure, and perceptions of form. Such a trainee is never again reborn in a lower realm. An ordinary being who reaches the peak of existence is still bound by the four yokes and will return. Master Cháng Bǎi: for them it is temporary suppression, not severance.
"Giving increases merit; guarding dissolves enmity; cultivating good relinquishes evil; the exhaustion of affliction attains nirvāṇa."

The prose: a householder with faith, free of stinginess, practises seven kinds of meritorious giving, and merit grows. A renunciant guards the precepts with patience; struck or abused, says no harsh word, and pervades all directions with loving-kindness, and enmity ceases. Through the three trainings, one realises the truths and leaves bad destinies behind; and gradually cutting all fetters, attains nirvāṇa with and then without remainder. Master Cháng Bǎi quotes a folk verse on anger: "Step forward three paces and think; step back three paces and reflect."
"Do not commit any evil; uphold and practise every good; tame your own mind completely: this is the teaching of all buddhas."

The prose: one with faith stops every wrong in every form, cause, and place; practises good through the three trainings; and tames the mind through three steps: knowing as it is, therefore disenchantment; disenchantment, therefore dispassion; dispassion, therefore liberation. In brief: the three trainings and their fruit, a teaching shared with no other tradition. Master Cháng Bǎi: "every good" includes precepts, concentration, and wisdom; taming the mind is their fruit.

quiz.q: According to the eighteenth verse, how does one cast off the four yokes and not be reborn?
options: purging all rumination, inwardly free of discrimination without remainder, passing beyond the obstructions and the perceptions of form
reciting for rebirth in a pure land
quiz.why: "If one purges every rumination, becomes, within, entirely free of discursive thought, and passes beyond every obstruction of perceptions tied to form — the four yokes cast off, one is reborn there no more." Master Cháng Bǎi: 蠲 means to cast off; a yoke is originally what is fastened on an ox.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain 蠲 and 軛?
options: 蠲 means to cast off; a yoke, originally on an ox, stands for four states that bind one
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: 蠲 is to cast off — casting off four states that bind oneself; yokes were originally fastened on oxen. Venerable Miào Jìng: having attained these four states, one is trapped by them — hence "yokes."

quiz.q: Ordinary meditators can also reach the peak of existence. Why are they still bound by the four yokes, per the two masters?
options: they only temporarily suppress affliction without severing the seeds; after eighty thousand eons they return to the desire realm
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: in this state they are still bound by the four yokes, because this is only temporary suppression of affliction, not ultimate severance of its seeds. Venerable Miào Jìng: they are still bound by the four yokes — only temporarily subdued, not truly free.

quiz.q: What four practices does the nineteenth verse name, and what does each achieve?
options: generosity increases merit; guarding against wrong dissolves enmity; cultivating good relinquishes evil; exhausting affliction attains nirvāṇa
giving for fame, precepts for long life
quiz.why: "Generosity increases merit; guarding against wrongdoing dissolves enmity and harm; cultivating what is wholesome relinquishes every evil; and the exhaustion of affliction attains nirvāṇa." Master Cháng Bǎi: to go from ordinary faith to pure faith one must cultivate these four right practices.

quiz.q: To explain "guarding against wrong dissolves enmity," Master Cháng Bǎi tells of a merchant who bought a verse. What was it?
options: "Step forward three paces and think; step back three paces and reflect; when anger rises, consider it — quenching that fire is most auspicious"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the verse was "Step forward three paces and think it over; step back three paces and reflect; when anger rises, consider carefully; quenching the fire of rage is most auspicious." Venerable Miào Jìng: if you harm me and I harm you, the enmity between us never ceases.

quiz.q: What four lines make up the twentieth verse, the teaching shared by no other tradition?
options: do no evil, practice all good, tame your own mind — this is the teaching of all buddhas
quiz.why: "Do not commit any evil; uphold and practice every good; tame your own mind completely — this is the teaching of all buddhas." Master Cháng Bǎi: discipline is the method of restraining evil, and decorum is conduct conforming to it.

quiz.q: The note assigns the three lines to precepts, concentration, and wisdom, then says the second line contains all three. How do the masters map them?
options: Cháng Bǎi: practising good includes all three trainings, and taming the mind is their fruit; Miào Jìng: the three lines are the fruit of the three trainings
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "uphold and practice every good" should include precepts, concentration, and wisdom; "tame your own mind" is the fruit of the three trainings. Venerable Miào Jìng: these three lines are the fruit of training in the three trainings.
